measurement.happened:
THE WAR AND STRIKES: The dominant story this week was a brutal escalation of mutual strikes between Russia and Ukraine, timed just days before US-brokered peace talks were to begin. Russia launched what multiple sources called 'massive' overnight strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, power substations, bridges, and civilian centers. Kyiv lost power to hundreds of thousands of residents, and the death toll from a single strike on an aid center in Zaporizhzhia region climbed to between 31 and 53 depending on the source and the day. Russia also hit a hospital, a hospice, and a school used as an aid center, and in a particularly grim episode, targeted emergency crews already responding to a bombing (a so-called double-tap strike). Zelensky and the Kyiv mayor publicly traded blame over the city's darkness. On the ground, the Wall Street Journal reported that in ten months of fighting Russia gained only 46 square miles, and Bloomberg noted that hacked records suggest around 400,000 Russian soldiers have been killed, with TV5Monde reporting 350 conscripts killed in a single period. Russia's land gains are dwindling. Ukraine, meanwhile, intensified its campaign against Russian oil refineries, hitting the Ryazan plant, the Saratov refinery, the Yanos refinery, and what NASA satellite imagery confirmed as a major oil hub on fire. Kyiv hit its sixth Russian oil plant in a single week, and Zelensky confirmed the campaign would continue. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 7 'Russia pounds power facilities around Kyiv'; AFP Nov 8 'Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands'; CNN Nov 8 'Putin appears set on wrecking Ukraine's economy'; Bloomberg Nov 6 'Kyiv Hits Sixth Russian Oil Plant in a Week'; BBC Nov 3 'Russian bombing kills 31 at aid centre'; Al Jazeera Nov 9 'At least four killed as Russia and Ukraine trade strikes overnight'; WSJ Nov 7 'Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles'.)

PEACE TALKS AND DIPLOMACY: The second major thread was the rapid build-up toward US-led trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, expected to begin around November 10. Trump met Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House and described the emerging framework as a 'big, beautiful' deal for all of Europe. Melania Trump positioned herself as an 'exclusive intermediary,' hosting both Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House to tout a local ceasefire. Russia upgraded its delegation for the talks, and European security agencies joined in an effort to shape the security-guarantee language. Trump said he expects to meet both Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in China, and China confirmed discussions are underway for that historic trilateral meeting. Iran's security chief met Putin and delivered a message from Khamenei, and a rocket-launcher deal deepened the Russia-Iran military tie. Turkey's Erdogan said he wants to discuss ending the war with Putin after talks with Zelensky. The Kremlin, however, accused Europe of struggling to decide who will speak for it at future security talks, and the EU's Kallas said Russia is 'pretending' to negotiate while 'bombing civilians.' (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 7 'Russian diplomats and military officials to join talks with US and Ukraine'; Bloomberg Nov 5 'Trump Meets Putin Envoy Kirill Dmitriev'; CNN Nov 5 'Melania Trump touts her diplomatic role'; FT Nov 9 'Europeans join Abu Dhabi talks'; Al Jazeera Nov 9 'No concession: What to expect from Russia-US-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi'; Reuters Nov 9 'Trump thinks he will meet Xi and Putin at China APEC summit'.)

RUSSIA'S FUEL AND ENERGY CRISIS: Ukrainian strikes on refineries are biting hard at home. Russia is rationing petrol in several regions, and diesel shortages have returned. Tankers carrying Russian diesel changed course, casting doubt on the US-Russia diesel deal that Trump had touted. The FT reported the deal is faltering as US fuel supplies hit a 20-year low. Russia's GDP grew only 1 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, and regions are cutting payments to families of fallen soldiers while the Defense Ministry delays pay amid a budget gap. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 9 'Fuel shortages return to Russian regions'; FT Nov 9 'Russia rations petrol after new Ukrainian strikes on refineries'; Bloomberg Nov 4 'Trump diesel deal with Russia falters'; Reuters Nov 5 'Russia's GDP grew 1% y/y in third quarter'; Bloomberg Nov 5 'Russian Regions Cut Payments to Families of Fallen Soldiers'.)

JAPAN TOBACCO SEIZURE: Putin ordered the seizure of Japan Tobacco's Russian business, expanding a temporary administration of its assets. Japan's stock market saw a second day of limit-down losses, and Tokyo formally protested. Bloomberg framed the grab as a risk to Prime Minister Takaichi's spending plan. Coca-Cola HBC said it received no notification from Russia on asset changes, hinting at more seizures to come. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 5 'Putin seizes control of Japan Tobacco's Russian assets'; Bloomberg Nov 7 'Russia Takes More Japan Tobacco Assets After Seizures Hit Shares'; Reuters Nov 8 'Japan Tobacco hit by second day of limit-down losses'; FT Nov 6 'Vladimir Putin orders seizure of Japan Tobacco's Russian business'.)

MEDIA AND INFORMATION WAR: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, officially closed its editorial office after three decades, citing official pressure. The Russian military began using deepfake videos to claim battlefield success. A covert Russian network was found to have exploited French riots on social media, according to an EU report. Pro-Russian hackers targeted Italy's foreign minister, and Estonia accused Russia of state-sponsored terrorism over a series of hybrid attacks. Both Russia and Ukraine reported that their emergency alert apps were hacked, with fake nuclear warnings sent to citizens in both countries. Rosstat, Russia's statistics agency, struggled to restore systems after a major cyberattack, and Belarusian hackers claimed to have obtained data on Russian military losses. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 9 'Lights go out at Russia's Novaya Gazeta'; FT Nov 9 'Russian military turns to deepfake videos'; Reuters Nov 9 'Covert Russian network exploited French riots'; BBC Nov 2 'Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked'; Bloomberg Nov 7 'Russia's Rosstat Struggles to Restore Systems After Major Cyberattack'.)

ICE HOCKEY DISPUTE: The Court of Arbitration for Sport ordered Russia's reinstatement into the World Junior Ice Hockey Championship, replacing Norway. Canada, Finland, and six other nations threatened or carried out boycotts. Putin said countries resisting Russia's return to world sport are 'violating democratic bodies.' Sponsors increased pressure on the IIHF. Germany, the host, demanded Russia be excluded. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 8 'Norway replaced by Russia for World Junior Championship after CAS ruling'; BBC Nov 4 'Canada bars Russia and Belarus from tournament'; Reuters Nov 5 'Putin says countries resisting Russia's return to world sport are violating democratic bodies'; Al Jazeera Nov 3 'Nordic nations refuse to face Russia in ice hockey'.)

EUROPEAN AND ALLIED REACTIONS: Poland arrested four people in a probe into military supplies sent to Russia and charged two more with supplying components. Finland's court convicted a Russian captain and an Azerbaijani crew member over Baltic Sea cable damage. Finland is considering Ukraine-style tank barriers as Russia rearms. Sweden said hybrid threats make internal border checks necessary. Bulgaria's pro-Russian candidate Yotova won the presidential runoff. Moldova launched a new power line to Romania to cut reliance on Russia. Serbia shut down a bank favored by Russians. The UK's military chief said the country must 'catch up' with Europe in opposing the Russian threat. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 5 'Poland arrest four in probe into military supplies sent to Russia'; Reuters Nov 5 'Finland court convicts Russian captain'; FT Nov 1 'Bulgaria's Russia-friendly Yotova wins presidential runoff'; Al Jazeera Nov 9 'Moldova launches new power line to Romania'; FT Nov 8 'UK must catch up with Europe in opposing Russian threat'.)

RUSSIA'S SPACE AND TECHNOLOGY PUSH: Russia is using its own version of Starlink for military communications over Ukraine, and its security council said the country must swiftly expand its answer to Musk's satellite constellation. Russia is racing to build a rival to Starlink. A specialist flagged that Russia may have rehearsed an attack on a satellite using a new approach. (Supporting headlines: Reuters Nov 6 'Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms'; FT Nov 8 'Russia races to build rival to Elon Musk's Starlink'; Reuters Nov 5 'Russia may have rehearsed attack on satellite'.)

Confidence: probable for continued diplomatic sparring; possible for another corporate seizure announcement.

MEDIA AND INFORMATION WARFARE (probable): Novaya Gazeta's closure will be a significant symbolic moment, and expect both Russian state media to frame it as a natural retirement while independent voices and Western outlets frame it as a loss. The deepfake videos and social-media manipulation campaigns will continue. The cyberattack on Rosstat will have follow-on effects on data releases. Expect at least one more incident involving hacked apps, leaked data, or a new hybrid-attack accusation from a Baltic or Nordic state. ICE HOCKEY DRAMA (probable): The World Junior Championship dispute will continue to generate headlines. Canada, Finland, and the six boycotting nations will hold their ground, and the IIHF will face mounting pressure. Putin may make another public statement defending Russia's right to compete. Sponsors may threaten to pull funding. This will be a low-stakes but high-noise story. Confidence: probable for continued public sparring; unlikely for a full resolution.

WINTER HEATING AND CIVILIAN IMPACT (possible): As November progresses and cold sets in, the damage to Ukraine's power and heating infrastructure will become more acute. Russia's own fuel shortages will make winter more uncomfortable for its citizens, especially in regions already rationing. Expect more public complaints and possibly local protests over heating and fuel prices. Confidence: possible for visible civilian impact; unlikely for major mass protests yet.

RUSSIA'S STARLINK RIVAL AND SPACE (possible): The security council's push to build a Starlink rival will likely produce at least one announcement or satellite launch in the coming days. The possible satellite-attack rehearsal, if confirmed, could lead to a brief diplomatic incident. Confidence: possible for an announcement; unlikely for a full launch in this window.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES: A sudden Russian ceasefire announcement timed to the Abu Dhabi talks (possible but not probable, given the pattern of striking before and during negotiations). A second major corporate seizure beyond Japan Tobacco (possible). A visible Russian protest or strike over fuel prices in a major city (unlikely but not impossible). A confirmed Russian satellite-attack test (possible). The APEC summit being formally scheduled with a date (probable as an announcement, even if the event itself is later).

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full peace deal or comprehensive ceasefire being signed in this window (unlikely). Russia accepting European security guarantees without major concessions (unlikely). A mass street protest in Moscow over fuel or the war (unlikely). The Novaya Gazeta closure being reversed or the team rehired (very unlikely). Russia launching a new major ground offensive to gain territory before the talks (unlikely given the momentum of the air campaign). A sudden Russian withdrawal from a contested position (very unlikely). Putin making a surprise personal visit to the US or China this week (unlikely; the APEC summit is still being arranged).
emoji_reasons: Russia's week was defined by massive airstrikes on Ukraine's energy grid and cities, with dozens killed, hundreds of thousands left without power, and a pattern of double-tap strikes on emergency crews, making the bombing the single most consequential event.

The rapid build-up to US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, Melania Trump's intermediary role, the Trump-Dmitriev meeting, and the planned Trump-Xi-Putin summit made peace diplomacy the week's central diplomatic thread, even as both sides kept striking.

Novaya Gazeta's closure after three decades, the deepfake battlefield videos, the hacked emergency apps in both countries, the EU report on Russian social-media manipulation of French riots, and the cyberattack on Rosstat together made the information and media war a defining undercurrent of the week.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the war's center of gravity shifted from a series of discrete, newsworthy events to a sustained, grinding escalation that is now the single dominant thread. In the first photograph, the Oleshky evacuation was the headline, the Russia-Africa Summit was the showcase, the G20 photo fiasco was the diplomatic drama, and the Novaya Gazeta closure was the media story. By the second photograph, Oleshky has almost vanished from the headlines, the Africa Summit has faded into a single Rosatom statement, and the G20 photo fiasco is a footnote. What has grown enormously is the physical violence of the war: where the first week featured a drone strike on a train station and a refinery fire, the second week brings overnight barrages on hospitals, hospices, aid centers, and a double-tap strike on emergency crews, with a death toll at a single Zaporizhzhia aid center climbing past thirty. Ukraine's counter-campaign against Russian refineries has also accelerated from one strike on Bashneft to six oil plants hit in a single week, and the consequences are now visible inside Russia: petrol rationing in several regions, diesel shortages returning, and the Trump-brokered diesel deal visibly faltering. A new and powerful theme has appeared that was barely present in the first photograph: Russia's domestic economic pain. GDP growth of one percent, regions cutting payments to soldiers' families, the Defense Ministry delaying pay, and the Japan Tobacco seizure all signal a state reaching into new pockets for revenue. The information war has also expanded dramatically. The first photograph showed Novaya Gazeta announcing its closure; the second shows it officially dark, the military deploying deepfake battlefield videos, both countries' air-alert apps hacked to send fake nuclear warnings, Rosstat struggling to recover from a cyberattack, and a covert Russian network exploiting French riots on social media. The diplomatic track, which in the first week was a collection of back-channel signals (CIA Director in Moscow, a phone call with Finland and Norway, Trump saying a meeting would be 'set up soon'), has compressed into a concrete, imminent trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi around November 10, with Trump personally meeting Putin's envoy Dmitriev, Melania positioning herself as an exclusive intermediary, and European security agencies scrambling to shape the security-guarantee language. The space theme has grown from a personal moment (Putin calling Musk a genius) to a structural rivalry: Russia is now flying its own Starlink alternative for military communications over Ukraine, racing to build a full constellation, and possibly rehearsing a satellite attack. The European reaction has broadened from two sabotage arrests in Germany and one plot in Romania to a wave of concrete actions: Poland arresting four and charging two more, Finland convicting a Russian captain, Bulgaria electing a pro-Russian president, Moldova building a new power line to Romania, Serbia shutting a Russian-favored bank, and Estonia accusing Russia of state-sponsored terrorism. What has shrunk or vanished is the sense that Russia is on the offensive in diplomacy. The Africa Summit, the G20 presence, the Musk-Putin handshake, the shadow-fleet logistics stories, and the New Jersey diesel drama have all receded. In their place is a Russia that is more defensive, more rationing, more hacking, and more desperate to get a favorable deal before the next wave of refinery strikes makes the pain public.
delta.wind: Theme by theme, the expectation was broadly right on direction but consistently too gentle on intensity and too optimistic on some specific outcomes. The Oleshky aftermath was expected to 'continue to dominate' Russian and Ukrainian media, but it largely evaporated within a week, replaced by the much larger Zaporizhzhia aid-center strike and the general escalation. The expectation was wrong here: the evacuation was a one-week story, not a sustained thread, and the Kremlin did not use it to expand the truce. The G20 friction was expected to fuel a week of European maneuvering, and that happened, but in a different form: the photo fiasco faded, and the friction moved into the Abu Dhabi talks, where Kallas accused Russia of 'pretending' to negotiate and the Kremlin complained Europe cannot decide who speaks for it. The Novaya Gazata closure was expected to trigger commentary and maybe a small protest; the closure did happen officially, but the bigger story was the broader information-war escalation (deepfakes, hacked apps, Rosstat cyberattack) that the expectation did not capture. The Ukraine war strikes were expected to include 'at least one major strike with significant casualties,' and that came true in spades, with multiple strikes on hospitals, schools, and aid centers and a death toll well above thirty in a single incident. The expectation that Ukraine would target refineries was right, but the scale (six plants in a week, NASA-confirmed fires) and the domestic consequence (rationing, the diesel deal faltering) went further than the forecast. The Russia-Africa follow-up was rated 'possible' for specific events, and it largely did not materialize; the summit was a political showcase, not the start of a sustained news cycle. The energy and oil theme was expected to keep generating headlines, and it did, but the expectation underplayed how much the refinery strikes would hurt Russia at home: the first photograph saw freight-rate stories and a New Jersey governor's threat, while the second shows actual petrol rationing, a faltering diesel deal, and a one-percent GDP print. The European sabotage and espionage theme was rated 'possible' for a minor follow-up incident, and the reality was a week's worth of arrests, convictions, a new president in Bulgaria, a new power line in Moldova, and a bank closure in Serbia. The US-Russia channel was expected to show 'a concrete step toward a trilateral meeting' but the meeting itself 'unlikely within this week.' The meeting is now scheduled for roughly November 10, one day after the second photograph, so the expectation was right on the direction and slightly too conservative on the timing. The less-likely surprises mostly did not happen: no nuclear exercise, no major cyberattack on a single European country (though several minor ones landed), no surprise Putin meeting with a European leader, and no Black Sea attack on a Turkish or Bulgarian vessel. Among the things the expectation said it would not bet on, the Japan Tobacco seizure stands out as a genuine surprise: a major new asset grab that hit Japanese markets and hinted at more seizures to come, with no signal in the first photograph. The 400,000 Russian soldier deaths from hacked records and the 46-square-miles-in-ten-months figure from the Wall Street Journal are also new data points that sharpen the picture of a war that is grinding and costly for Russia. Melania Trump's self-appointment as 'exclusive intermediary' and the Russia-Iran rocket-launcher deal are additional threads that the expectation did not anticipate. Overall, the expectation framework was sound in identifying the major themes, but it systematically underestimated the pace of escalation in the war, the speed at which the diplomatic track would compress into a concrete meeting, and the degree to which the economic pain of the war would become visible inside Russia within a single week.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a military that is running out of time, territory, and bodies, and a political leadership that is still negotiating as if it holds the upper hand. The Wall Street Journal's figure of forty-six square miles gained in ten months and the hacked records suggesting four hundred thousand Russian soldiers killed are not just statistics; they are the arithmetic that makes every refinery strike on Ukrainian soil feel like a punch to the chest in Moscow, because the fuel that was supposed to keep the war machine and the civilian economy running is now being rationed in regions, the diesel deal with the United States is faltering, and the Defense Ministry is delaying pay. At the same time, the diplomatic window has opened just wide enough to matter: Abu Dhabi is weeks away, Trump is personally courting the deal, Melania is inserting herself into the process, and Europe is scrambling to get a seat at the table. Russia is trying to lock in a favorable framework before the next wave of strikes makes its economic weakness public, and the information war (deepfakes, hacked alert apps, the Novaya Gazata closure, the covert network in France) is the tool it is using to control the narrative in that narrow window. The Japan Tobacco seizure, the Bulgaria presidential win, the Moldova power line, and the Serbia bank closure are all small moves in a broader pattern of a state that is tightening its grip on foreign assets and its neighbors' economies while it negotiates. The driver, in short, is a country that is losing the war on the ground faster than it is winning it at the table, and every week it spends without a deal makes the next one harder to negotiate from.

crystal.headline: Abu Dhabi Talks Open as Russia and Ukraine Trade Devastating Strikes
emoji_reasons: The US-brokered trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi are the single most consequential diplomatic event of the week, with Trump, Europe, and Russia all converging on a framework.
Mutual strikes on energy, hospitals, and refineries will continue to escalate, with Russia hitting civilian targets and Ukraine striking its sixth and seventh refineries.
Russia's domestic fuel crisis is deepening with petrol rationing, diesel shortages, and a faltering US diesel deal, making the energy pain visible in every region.
crystal.tldr: The US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi will open around November 10, generating intense diplomatic headlines but no formal breakthrough, while Russia and Ukraine continue to trade devastating strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure. Russia's fuel crisis will deepen with petrol rationing spreading to more regions, and the Japan Tobacco seizure will prompt at least one more foreign asset grab. The information war will expand with new deepfakes, cyberincidents, and the aftermath of the Novaya Gazeta closure.
crystal.eli5:
Next week, the big story is a meeting in Abu Dhabi where the US, Russia, and Ukraine sit down to talk about ending the war. President Trump is very excited about it and calls it a 'big beautiful deal,' and his wife Melania is trying to be a peacemaker too. But Russia and Ukraine are still bombing each other hard while they talk, so don't expect them to shake hands and sign a paper. Think of it like two kids arguing in a classroom while the teacher tries to get them to make up: they'll talk, they'll say some nice things, but they probably won't fully solve their problem yet.

At the same time, Russia is running out of gas, literally. Ukraine has been bombing Russian oil refineries nonstop, and now regular people in Russian cities can't find enough petrol or diesel to drive their cars or heat their homes. It's like if your local gas station ran out of fuel for the third week in a row. The Russian government is trying to hide how bad it is, but the cracks are showing: they're cutting pay for soldiers' families, and the economy is barely growing.

There's also a lot of drama in the information world. Russia just shut down its last big independent newspaper, and the military is making fake videos that look real to show off battlefield wins. Both Russia and Ukraine had their phone alert apps hacked, so people got fake warnings that a nuclear bomb was coming. It's like if your school's emergency alert system started going off for no reason, and then someone made a fake video of the principal saying the school was on fire. Everyone gets confused and a little scared.

And in a smaller but weird story, a court in Switzerland said Russia gets to play in the junior ice hockey championship, and now Canada, Finland, and several other countries are threatening to boycott the whole tournament. Putin is mad and says the countries that don't want Russia to play are 'violating democratic bodies,' which is like a kid in a playground saying the other kids are breaking the rules of the game just because they don't want him to play.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A captured several of the week's major threads correctly. Its 'almost certain' call on continued strikes and counter-strikes on energy infrastructure was spot-on: Russia hit power plants, bridges, aid centers, and hospitals with devastating casualties (31 to 53 killed at a single aid center, 26 at another, a double-tap on emergency crews), while Ukraine struck six Russian refineries in a week. The Novaya Gazeta closure generating sustained commentary and some domestic reaction was also well called. The diesel/tanker drama played out as predicted, with the deal faltering, tankers changing course, and US fuel supplies hitting a 20-year low. The European espionage and hybrid-war thread materialized across multiple countries: Poland arrests, Finland's conviction of a Russian captain, Estonia's state-sponsored terrorism accusation, pro-Russian hackers targeting Italy's foreign minister, and the fake nuclear warnings via hacked emergency apps in both countries. The US-Russia back-channel activity was present, though Forecast A rated it only 'possible' when the talks were actually confirmed and delegations named. The Oleshky aftermath continued but was not as dominant as Forecast A's 'almost certain' framing suggested; it faded into the background within a few days, which is closer to what the diplomatic track absorbed. The G20/Western Sahara angle (Putin not invited to Manchester, the Western Sahara peacekeeping mission ending after 35 years) was a legitimate but minor thread. The Russia-Africa follow-up was present but not a headline driver. What Forecast A missed entirely: the Japan Tobacco seizure, which was a major story spanning multiple days and hitting Japan's stock market with limit-down losses; the CAS ice hockey ruling and the multi-country boycott that generated a large cluster of headlines; the domestic fuel rationing in Russian regions; the Russia-Iran rocket-launcher deal and deepening military ties; the US midterms' political impact on the Ukraine track; and the prominent Melania Trump diplomatic role, which was a bigger story than the generic 'US-Russia channels' framing captured. The 400,000 Russian casualties figure and the 46-square-miles-gained-in-ten-months data point were significant context that neither forecast flagged. Overall, Forecast A's picture was broadly correct on the major war, diplomacy, media, and espionage threads, but it was scattered, with too many 'possible' items competing for attention and insufficient precision on the diplomatic track's actual state.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B was more tightly structured and its confidence calibrations were generally better matched to what actually happened. Its 'high confidence' call on the Abu Dhabi talks being in final logistics, with the talks landing on the last day or just after, was precisely right: the talks were confirmed for around November 10, delegations were named, Russia upgraded its team, and Europeans joined in a bid to shape security-guarantee language. The espionage and hybrid-war section correctly anticipated the geographic spread widening, and the actual week delivered incidents in Poland, Finland, Estonia, Italy, and the cross-border fake nuclear warning hack. The space/Starlink thread as a 'low-moderate' background item was accurate: Russia was using its own satellite constellation for military comms over Ukraine, the security council called for a swift Starlink rival, and a satellite-attack rehearsal was flagged. What Forecast B missed: the Japan Tobacco seizure (a major multi-day story with Japan protests, limit-down stock losses, and the Coca-Cola HBC no-notification follow-up); the CAS ice hockey ruling and the boycott cascade; the Russia-Iran rocket-launcher deal; the US midterms' political implications; and the 400,000-casualties / 46-square-miles data points. judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the dominant threads of the week: the brutal escalation of mutual strikes timed just before the talks, the diplomatic build-up toward Abu Dhabi, the Novaya Gazeta closure, the energy/diesel saga, and the spread of European hybrid-war incidents. Both missed the Japan Tobacco seizure and the ice hockey/CAS dispute, which together accounted for a significant share of the week's headlines. The key differentiator is precision and calibration. Forecast B's Abu Dhabi section was more specific and better calibrated: it correctly identified the talks as being in 'final logistics phase' with the meeting landing 'on the very last day of the window or just after it,' which matched reality almost exactly. Forecast A's US-Russia section rated the back-channel activity as merely 'possible' and did not name Abu Dhabi or the Melania Trump hosting role, underselling what was actually the week's second-largest diplomatic story. Forecast B's diesel section was more concrete about the political fight and the tanker logistics, and while the specific New Jersey enforcement drama was less prominent than the broader 'deal faltering' narrative, the direction was right. Forecast A's energy section was more general. On the war, both were correct, but Forecast B's note about a potential large Ukrainian refinery strike reversing the coverage asymmetry was a sharper prediction that matched the six-refinery-in-a-week campaign. On the post-Oleshky story, Forecast B's prediction that it would fade within two to three days was more accurate than Forecast A's 'almost certain' framing that it would continue to dominate. Forecast A's G20/Western Sahara angle was a legitimate minor thread but did not significantly affect the week's center of gravity. Forecast B's overall structure was more coherent, its confidence levels were better matched to outcomes, and it would have given a reader a clearer, more actionable picture of the week's likely shape. Forecast A covered more ground but at the cost of precision, and its 'almost certain' on Oleshky dominance was an overcall. The gap is not huge, but Forecast B's tighter focus and better calibration give it the edge. VERDICT: B
